turns.summary: return HTTP 409 on an optimistic-lock version conflict during concurrent update
turns.content: When a write supplies a stale version, the update is rejected with HTTP 409 Conflict and a problem body code ORDER_VERSION_CONFLICT. The client should re-read, re-apply, and retry. 409 is reserved specifically for optimistic concurrency conflicts on the same record.

upstream HTTP calls use a 2 second timeout
turns.content: Outbound HTTP calls to upstream services have a hard 2s timeout. Exceeding it aborts the call and surfaces a 504 to the caller. This is separate from the database statement timeout. 2s was chosen to keep p99 request latency under the 1s SLO budget with one retry.

service-to-service authentication uses mutual TLS (mTLS) with rotating certs
turns.content: Internal service-to-service calls authenticate with mTLS; each service has a SPIFFE identity and certs rotate every 24h via the mesh. This is distinct from end-user auth, which uses JWTs. mTLS means a compromised user token cannot be replayed between internal services.

prevent lost updates from concurrent writes with optimistic locking via a version column
turns.content: Each mutable row has an integer version column. Updates carry the read version in a WHERE clause and bump it; a zero-row update means a concurrent writer won, so the service returns 409 and the client retries. No long-held pessimistic locks. This is how we prevent lost updates under concurrency.

turns.summary: rows are soft-deleted via a deleted_at timestamp, never hard-deleted online
turns.content: Deletion sets deleted_at to now() and filters it out of normal reads. Hard deletion happens only in an offline retention job after 90 days. Soft-delete preserves audit history and lets us undo accidental deletes.

event delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must tolerate duplicates
turns.content: The platform guarantees at-least-once delivery: an event may be delivered more than once on retry or rebalance. Exactly-once was rejected as too costly. Consumers are responsible for idempotency. Ordering is per-partition only.

turns.summary: consumers achieve idempotency by deduplicating on an event dedup key
turns.content: Each event carries a stable dedup key (producer id + sequence). Consumers record processed keys in a short-TTL store and skip a key they have already handled, so a redelivered event is a no-op. This is how we avoid processing the same event twice.
